speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to say a few words in this debate, I wish to join with previous speakers in extending to you, Sir, my most hearty congratulations upon your promotion to the high office which you now occupy. I feel satisfied that I am only expressing the sentiments of hon. gentlemen on both sides1 of the House when I say that I feel confident that you will discharge the duties of this high and honourable position with that ability and impar-
390 '

tiality which have characterized your distinguished predecessors.
I regretted very much to hear some of my hon. friends on this side of the House make the complaint that in the selection of regimental officers, and other officials of the Militia Department, in their respective constituencies, discrimination was shown against those of their friends who might be of the Liberal persuasion. I am glad to say that in the county of Kent, a portion of which I have the honour to represent in this House, appointments such as have been described have not been made. When companies were formed by the Militia Department, the officers were selected from the very best- men regardless of their political opinions.
I am proud to say that when the first contingent left Canada we sent a couple of companies from the county of Kent, and the .man in charge was Major George Smith, a Liberal in politics. He fought at the front with his men behind him on many occasions, and I am sorry .to inform the House that in the last great battle in which he was engaged he was killed while attacking a third trench after he and his men had already captured two. I wish to extend to the Prime Minister of this country and to the Minister of Militia the most sincere thanks of my constituents, as well as my own, for the kind letters of condolence that they extended to Major Smith's wife and orphan son. I am glad to inform the House that since that time many of the brightest young men in the county of Kent have left for the front to do battle in defence of their country-not only men in the humbler walks of life, but sons of our wealthiest families in the city of Chatham, and in the municipalities and in the whole county. I am also glad to say that the ladies of Kent county have at all times endeavoured to do their duty. Whether in connection with the Red Cross Society, the Daughters of the Empire, or some other patriotic association, the ladies of my county, like the many ladies we see at different times in the galleries of this building, are providing comforts for those who have gone to the front, working from the time they get up in the morning till they go to bed at night. The ladies in the country districts in the county of Kent went so far last harvest as to can hundreds and hundreds of qparts of peaches and forwarded them to the front, and the boys at the front have expressed their appreciation not 
only for the fruit that has been sent them, but for the many other acts of kindness which have been extended to them by the industrious women of Kent. The fund which was provided to look after the boys at the front from the county has, I am glad to say, on no occasion been exhausted. I see by the Patriotic Bulletin, issued under the direction of the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames), that Kent county raised $85,000 in three days for the Patriotic Fund. Furthermore, Mr. Harry Collins, the local treasurer of the fund, has assured Sir Herbert Ames that the city of Chatham and county promised $150,000 for the year 1916. I think we all admire Sir Herbert Ames. He has given much of his time and attention to the Patriotic Fund, and as its secretary enjoys the confidence, I believe, of all members of this House and of the people as a whole. When he visited Chatham he was received there in the most unpartisan way imaginable, and he said that the county had contributed even more generously than the figures showed, as they had previously spent the sum of $15,000 for the use of the wives and dependents of the soldiers who had enlisted at an earlier date.
I am also glad to inform the House that the Minister of Militia has given instructions to form a Kent battalion, known as the 186th, for overseas service, and they have already obtained some three or four hundred splendid fellows. The man at the * head of that battalion is Lt. Colonel Neil Smith, a Liberal. The Minister of Militia appointed him befcause he knew that he was the best man that could be found for the position, not only in the county of Kent, but possibly in the whole of Ontario. The Minister of Militia knew him personally. Lt. Colonel Neil Smith is such an expert marksman that he was chosen for the Bisley team which went to England some years ago, and he did honour to the county of Kent while he was there, for he carried off some of the highest prizes.- He was selected to go with the Bisley team on another occasion, and I am proud to say that in competition with the greatest marksmen in the Empire he was second in the competition for the highest prize awarded. He not only brought honour on himself, and on the Minister of Militia who appointed him, but upon the Dominion of Canada, the county of Kent, and will say, also, on the new battalion which is now being formed. When the day comes for this battalion to leave Canada, Lt. Colonel

Smith will have associated with him as officers some of the brightest young men that ever breathed the breath of life, Liberals and Conservatives, and I doubt whether a finer fighting force will be found than the 186th Kent Battalion. When the occasion presents itself at the front I know that the 186th will do themselves proud, and do the Empire proud. I say this in all seriousness; in the county of Kent we fight elections as keenly as in any other section of Canada, but when the elections are over politics are forgotten, and we work for the very best interests of the county. As far as great industries in the city of Chatham are concerned, if the Prime Minister were in his seat he would bear me out in saying that Chatham has the very best industries of any city of its size in the wlhole Dominion. I remember well the Premier paying us a visit during the elections of 1911. On that occasion I had the privilege of hearing the right hon. gentleman address one of the largest meetings ever held in the county, and he paid one of the highest compliments to our industries that has ever been paid by any statesman or leader of any great political party.
I do not remember his words exactly, but he was so impressed with our industries and the agricultural district surrounding the city of Chatham that when he came back to headquarters in Ottawa he insisted upon the Minister of Finance paying us a visit, also the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Justice, and, as regards members on the back benches, the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. J. E. Armstrong), the hon. member for East Peterborough (Mr. Sexsmith), and the hon. Mr. Good-eve, who represented Kootenay at that time, but has since been promoted. All these gentlemen came to see the splendid industries established in the city of Chatham and the splendid agricultural sections surrounding it. After they had done their part in paying compliments to our splendid city and county, we also had a visit from: Sir Clifford Sifton and Mr. Arthur Hawkes, who also paid their respects to the people of the county of Kent, and I am sure that all these hon. gentlemen will hear me out when I say that no honest Government could conscientiously, if they considered for a moment the industries in the county of Kent, let contracts as they have done by the hundreds of millions of dollars and overlook that county and city of which they said they were so proud,
when they paid us those complimentary visits at that particular time. Contracts for shells and 'boxes have been let not only in the city of St. Thomas, which the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) has the honour of representing, but in the city of London, in the town of Ingersoll; but when the Shell Committee came down the Grand Trunk line, they missed the city of Chatham, jumped over to the town of Walker-ville, and gave that town a big contract. As we had some industries that were lying idle, that could manufacture shells or other goods required by the Militia Department for the carrying on of this war, we sent deputation after deputation of the very best citizens of the city of Chatham to wait on the different members of the Government and on other men connected with it Who, we thought, might persuade the Government to give our manufacturers some work, because a number of our factories were closing down and a number of men capable of doing work along this particular line were anxious for,employment. As proud, however, as all these ministers of the Government and their colleagues were of the city of Chatham, not one dollar's worth of shells or boxes was given to that beautiful city. Seeing that they had visited the city, I thought that it would be well for me to write the Minister of Labour, believing that he would have the, patronage of the southwestern part of Ontario. I received from that hon. gentleman a very kind letter in which he asked me to write to Colonel Bertram. I took advantage of his suggestion and wrote to Colonel Bertram, and I received a reply from the colonel assuring me that the contracts were all awarded for the shells that were needed at that particular time, but that he would not overlook Chatham at the very earliest opportunity when there were any shell contracts to be let, and that our manufacturers could be sure that they would get their share. While at that time we were in need of work for our labouring men, who are as good a class of mechanics and labourers as are to be found in the province of Ontario, we were unable to get work for them, and all I have to say is this, that thanks to the progressive board of trade and the council and certain intelligent citizens of the city of Chatham, those factories which at that time were in need of contracts to make shells and boxes are going to be working full blast, and our labouring men will be employed without any thanks to the present Administration. We enjoy to-day the proud distinction of being one of

the cities that have not gone back at this time of financial stress and trouble, and our city is going to go ahead. In the near future a large sugar plant will be erected which will mean the expenditure of about a million dollars, and other industries are being established at .the present time. And I simply want to assure this Government that 'as far as the city of Chatham is concerned, even if they cannot see their way clear to give us. any contracts or any work, the labouring men as well as the manufacturers throughout the county will do everything in their power to put up money and to send men to assist this Government in bringing to a successful conclusion the war which is now raging.
. I was particularly pleased to hear the hon. Minister of Militia the other afternoon when he addressed this House make the following statement, as reported on page 304 of Hansard:
Let us take up next the Militia appointments. Two divisional commanders out of three are good staunch Liberals. I refer to General Currie, of Victoria, and to General Turner, of Quebec, two of the finest fellows who ever stood inside jackets, and two of the best men to be found in the Dominion.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier: Hear, hear.
Sir Sam Hughes: Not a solitary Conservative in the Whole Dominion objected when I nominated these men for brigadiers long ago. The other one is General Mercer. As regards the politics of the brigadiers, I understand they are about half and half. I do not know what my own son's politics may be, but I know he will vote straight anyway. As regards the lower commanders, I am told by those who ****<. looked up the matter-I have not looked up myself, it would make no difference anyway-that three-fourths of them are Liberal and one-fourth Tory.
It is gratifying to me as one of the younger members of this House to hear the Minister of Militia give not only to the members of this House but to the people throughout the length and breadth [DOT]of Canada, the assurance that the Liberal party is doing its share in sending men and officers to assist in this great struggle. There are some who make invidious comparisons, men who we sometimes say belong to the flag-waving party. These men, in. the face of this announcement, will never again dare to say that the Liberal party in this great struggle is not doing its duty in the way of supplying officers, when we already have three out of four commanding the different companies and regiments.	.
On this and on other occasions there have come up matters to which almost every speaker has referred, and there is one which is certainly very ahiusing. 
Speakers on the opposite side, and on this side, are all referring, Sir, to two gentlemen from your native province, Mr. Bourassa and Mr. Lavergne, and they all seem to be trying to drop them like two hot coals. In the constituency which I represent, one of the great points made during the campaign at the last general election was that all that the Conservatives needed was to win twenty-two seats. In the Conservative paper of my city, on the night when the hon. Minister of Finance addressed the electors in my riding, there was quite a long article saying that twenty-two seats would win the election for Sir Robert Borden, and in the report of that meeting in the paper there was given a summary of how it could be accomplished; that is, that Mr. Bourassa would carry many seats in Quebec, because the fight was not on the reciprocity issue,	but the great issue
was that the people of Quebec were opposed to Laurier and his navy. This was the argument they were putting up-that they would carry so many seats in Ontario, so many seats in the Maritime Provinces and the West, and Bourassa would carry so many .seats in Quebec, and this would put the Conservatitve party into power. Let me assure hon. gentlemen that, so far as the county of Kent is concerned, on patriotic lines we are a united people, and will do everything possible to assist this Government in carrying on our share of the war.
Many references have been made to the speech of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), especially in the speech of the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell), whom I am glad to see in his place. I feel that I speak for every hon. member on this side of the House when I assure the hon. minister that so far as he is personally concerned we regard him as one of the finest gentlemen we have in this House at this time. I believe the member for Carleton rendered a great service not only to this Parliament hut also to the agriculturists of Canada in placing before this House the charges he made with regard to the contracts in his own province. It is greatly to the credit of the hon. member for Carleton that he at last woke up the Minister of Agriculture to deliver a speech with the fire and vim that the minister displayed. If the minister would only follow up his great agitation of a year ago for "Patriotism and Production" with the same force and energy that he displayed

in his abuse of the hon. member for Car-leton, it would be a great blessing for the agriculturists of Canada. What has the hon. mimilster been doing itttie iasit two or three sessions? I put that question to the respected colleagues of the hon. minister. The charge is made that a contract has been entered into for 15,000 tons of hay at $23 a ton. I cannot understand why the members on the Conservative side of the House, particularly those from the province of Ontario, elected by the agriculturists of that province, will sit in their places and pound their desks when the minister announces a contract of this kind, when there are tons upon tons of hay in the province of Ontario for which we cannot get more than $12 or $13 a ton. No person knows better than I do that if one cannot get a market for his products it is mighty little use to grow them. But if the minister wished to contract for 15,000 tons of hay-I put this to hon. gentlemen on the other side who are interested in agriculture-would it not have been better to divide that up into two or three contracts of moderate size and give to the farmers of Ontario-of whom we are so proud at election times particularly, and to whom we always/appeal for support-an opportunity to supply the requirements? In the southwestern part of Ontario we have the best hay-producing section in this whole dominion.

Out of respect to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux), I will revise that, and say that we can produce hay equally good and in equally large quantities with any other section of the Dominion. But * if we can not sell our hay to the Government or to the people of our own large cities, then, if we see a market across the line, we want the privilege of sending our hay to that market. But what has happened? This contract is let at $23 a ton to friends of the Government-that is not denied by the minister-and the very minute that contract is let an embargo is put upon hay so that it can not be sent out of this country. That simply means that the Minister of Agriculture was neglecting the men whom he is alleged to represent in this House.
In the same way, on the first day of May last, a very similar thing was done by this Government when it passed an order in council placing an embargo on wool. The Minister of Agriculture-

I appeal to you, Mr. Speaker-you have been one of my old friends on the ball ground. The hon. member for North Essex had his innings the other day, and I think the House will allow me my innings to-day. I say that on the first day of May last an embargo was placed upon wool, and I appeal to the Minister of Agriculture if that is not so. This was in the warm season when the farmers were shearing their sheep-at any rate that was the case in my own constituency. Now, naturally, farmers in humble circumstances do not know the minds of this Government and of the Minister of Agriculture. They naturally thought that this embargo was put on for keeps. They would not suppose that it was done for a joke. These farmers assumed that this was a business act by business men. And so they went on and sold their-wool. At the time the embargo was put on the price of wool was 30 cents a pound. On 8th May it was 20-25 cents; on 15th May it was down to 20 cents, and the same on 22nd May. But the agricultural papers of the province of Ontario put up such a fight that the minister could not stand it, and so he put the embargo off. Immediately the price went back to 25 cents, and by 25th June it was 35 cents. The difference in price between this date and the time when the embargo was on was 15 cents a pound, and who was the loser? The loser was the man in humble circumstances, wherever he may live throughout the length and breadth of Canada, who was engaged in the sheep industry. The loss of the average man in this matter was enough to have paid his hired man for the season.	.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the
House rose at six o'clock I was endeavouring to draw to the attention of the Hon. Minister of Agriculture some of the reasons why I felt that he should look into many parts of his department and try to make some alterations which would be greatly to the benefit of the farmers whom he represents in this House. I had finished my references to the question of placing an embargo on wool. There is now another matter which I should like to draw to the attention of the House, and that is the tobacco industry.
We have in the county of Kent, and also in the adjoining counties, a great number of farmers who have been encouraged to go into the tobacco industry, and who have spent large sums of money on the advice 
of the Government of this country. About two years ago, after the farmers had invested large sums of money in that industry, and had endeavoured to put it on a paying basis, and give employment to a large number of labouring men who were looking for work in the different counties, I drew the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the fact that the farmers, who had grown the tobacco, had been unable to dispose of it and that they felt that the purchasing of that particular crop had been left too much in the hands of one buyer. In fact, it was alleged by these producers that there was a combine,- so far as the purchasing of tobacco was concerned, in the different southwestern counties of the province of Ontario. I drew the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the matter, feeling that he would be interested, or at all events should be interested, in the different agricultural industries which are carried on in all parts of the Dominion, and'that he should endeavour to do something to assist the farmers in that particular industry.
The reply I received from the minister, I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, was very cold consolation for the farmers to whom I referred. If I remember rightly, his letter referred me to the Minister of Labour, and told me that if there was a combine, the farmers could take the matter up under the Combines Act and possibly get some redress from that source. Whether the Department of Agriculture could do anything or not, it certainly did very little at that particular time in trying to assist the farmers who were engaged in the tobacco industry, or in endeavouring to find markets for the crops which they could not dispose of in that particular section of the country.
Time went on, things grew worse, and the farmers, feeling that they could not possibly continue in that industry unless something was done, made up their minds to come to Ottawa. They came to Ottawa and were received by hon. ministers of the Government. The Minister of Agriculture was absent, possibly unavoidably, at any rate he was not present, but I have never heard that he got any information from the ministers who received that delegation, or that he took any steps to assist them in the work in which they were interested. I can assure you, Sir, that on that occasion the deputation, which numbered between 200 and 300, and the members of which had paid their own fares from extreme points in the province of Ontario to Ottawa, and included many from the province of Quebec, went away after their courteous recep-

tion feeling that they would have some assistance from the Government of this country.	,
I remember the arguments that were advanced. They asked if the Government would change the excise duty to a customs duty. It was contended by the Minister of Finance, and by the other gentlemen who spoke on that occasion, that there was practically no difference .so far as that was concerned, They asked for other concessions. I remember well that some of the farmers argued that there was a great difference between an excise duty and w customs duty, and that if the Government said that their request would be granted they would go home perfectly satisfied, feeling that they had accomplished something as a result of their trip to the capital of the Dominion.
Shortly afterwards I remember the Minister of Finance summoned some manufacturers of this country to meet him. The manufacturers, who numbered possibly four or five, had an interview with the minister, but the 'Government has done practically nothing since; certainly, nothing has been heard so far as assisting the tobacco growers is concerned.
After their visit to Ottawa the Ontario producers met Quebec consumers, and were able, by their own efforts, to dispose of a portion of their crop which they had in their barrife at that particular time. The position is this: If the farmers cannot depend upon the Minister of Agriculture taking an interest in the crops which his department encourages the farmers to produce, to whom are the farmers to go for assistance in important matters of that kind? I understand that the people who are interested in this great industry are coming back to Ottawa to wait upon the 'Government again, and to see if there is not some possible way of assisting them. I hope that when they do return the Minister of Agriculture will be able to join his colleagues in receiving such an important body of men, and will see his way to give not only encouragement but some substantial assistance.
There-is another matter to which I wish to call the attention of the Government, particularly the Minister of Agriculture. There are many matters of importance connected with his department in which he seems to take very little interest. A year ago the farmers, not only of my county, but of other counties in the province of Ontario, were threatened with an epidemic of
hog cholera, which threatened to wipe out the hog industry. At that time the farmers connected with one of the farmers' institutes in my county wrote to the minister and asked him to come and wait upon them and discuss the situation with the view of suggesting measures which would save those interested in the hog industry from great financial loss. What happened on that occasion? The Minister of Agriculture replied to those farmers that he was too busy to come and meet them. He was too busy at that time to go to the county of Kent and discuss that important question which was causing financial loss, but he was not too busy a short time before that to go and address a Conservative convention in the city of Chatham. The farmers took the matter up and one of the veterinaries came to the city of Chatham and heard the arguments of the farmers, and he left with an entirely different view of the situation from fbjat he had formerly held. When the matter was brought up in this House, the Prime Minister made a note of the matter, and I believe he insisted upon the Minister of Agriculture taking steps to assist the hog industry. I repeat if you cannot depend on the Minister of Agriculture to look after the industries connected with his department, whom can we depend upon? A year ago the minister and his department, recommended the farmers to go in for wheat extensively. A few weeks ago I read in one of the Toronto papers an interview in which'the deputy minister advised them not to go into wheat-growing extensively, but to curtail their wheat crops and go into cattle raising extensively. The result is that today in the province of Ontario, and particularly in the section I come from, we' have not one-half the acreage in wheat which we had twelve months ago. What followed? The farmers curtailed their crops, and when the market opened they were receiving $1 a bushel for their wheat. A few farmers at that time disposed of it. I was one of the few who were fortunate enough to do so, and I got a dollar a bushel for a thousand bushels of wheat. But after that wheat began to drop; it went down from $1 to 95 cents, then 85 cents, then 80 cents, and finally as low as 75 cents a bushel. The men who were in humble circumstances in the province of Ontario had to dispose of their wheat at the smaller price. On the 24th November this Government commandeered 15,000,000 bushels of wheat. If my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture has the confidence of his col-

leagues he should have known that this wheat' was going to be commandeered in November. The minute that announcement was made by the Government the price ol wheat began to go up until to-day we see that May wheat is quoted at $1.35 a bushel. The farmers who, after threshing, were forced to sell their wheat to pay their taxes, their rent, the interest on their mortgages, the notes that they had given for the things which it was necessary for them to procure to enable them to conduct their business, and generally to meet their liabilities, had to dispose of their wheat, and these men who were	unable to	hold it for	thereasons I have enumerated, had to take a smaller	price	than that whichthe wealthy farmers, - millers and elevator men	were	able	to demand	forthe wheat	which	they	had in store.	We
had a larger acreage of wheat in the province than usual, largely because of the campaign which had been carried on in 1914. The farmers should have been advised that there would be this demand for wheat by the Minister of Agriculture, whose duty it is to give information to the people who are depending upon him. I was glad that my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B., (Mr. Carvell) woke up the Minister of Agriculture the other day to new life and vigour in this House, and I hope that an equal energy will characterize his administration of the department over which he presides.
Not only did the farmers in humble circumstances sustain a loss by the disposal of their wheat at this particular time, but the farmer has even a greater grievance against the Government than this. I refer to the scandals which have arisen in different parts of the country in connection with the^ purchase of horses for military purposes. The question of the purchase of horses by the Government was brought prominently before the House twelve months ago. After the late member for Kings, N.S., had been read out of the party by the right hon. the Prime * Minister, we expected that we would hear no more about members or supporters of the Government taking a prominent part in the purchasing of horses. A year or two ago, wftien a great many horses of an inferior quality were thrown upon the market, it was advertised in ithe press of the country that this was the class of horses that was being shipped from Canada for war purposes. As . far as the purchase of horses is concerned, we care not ihow much . was made by certain, men down in Kings
[M'. McC g.]
county, N.S., but we do complain that, as a consequence of these men throwing an inferior class of horses upon the market, in order to make a few dollars, the reputation of Canadian horses has, to a certain extent, been ruined, to the great injury of our legitimate farmers, wlho, for many years, on the advice not only of the present Government, but of previous governments, have been endeavouring to make the horse industry one, of the most important in this Dominion. But what do we find? We find that the same practices which occurred in Nova Scotia were repeated in Ontario. Considering the high regard- that we all have for the hon. gentleman who represents the constituency we would scarcely expect that a similar ambition would manifest itself there; but in the constituency of the hon. gentleman who represents the county of Peel (Mr. Blain) we find that the Conservative member of the Provincial Legislature gets a contract and goes into the horse-buying business also.
Now, let us see what the press of the country says about these particular transactions. First, I shall read from the Toronto World, a good Conservative paper, which, I am sure, my hon. friends opposite will not object to me quoting. The World says:
Tells Sir Charles Davidson, Royal Commissioner, of Sale of Horses for Army- * Some Rejected Sold-Albert Kee, Brampton Liveryman, Says Horses Turned Down, Accepted After.
Brampton, Dec. 1.-As a result of rumours that have been in circulation here for some time, an investigation regarding the buying of army horses in Peel county, dating back to August, 1914, was opened before Sir Charles Davidson, Royal Commissioner, here yesterday afternoon, John Thompson, K.C., of Ottawa, conducted the examination.
The first witness called was E. J. Jones, a horse dealer of Brampton. He had, in partnership with James E. Fallis, also of Brampton, sold 360 horses in August, 1914, to the government agents, Col. Hall and Capt. McDonald. Fallis financed the business and received two-thirds of the profits, one-third being his share.
To Mr. Thompson's inquiry as to the profits out of this sale of horses, Jones replied :
"About $3,200. I received $1,000 and my partner about $2,000."
This Mr. Fallis was a member of the Legislature, and he received $2,000 and his partner $1,000. That is where the trouble began again.
What did the Toronto News say about the investigation? I will just read the headlines. As every ihon. member of this House knows, this is one of the leading Conservative papers in the province: "

Fifteen-Year-Old Horse sold at Brampton for the Army-Sir Charles Davidson continues investigation into Purchases-'Deny Payments of Commission-One horse said to have been " fixed up " by Shoes.
I have another from the Toronto Star:
Davidson Probe at Brampton Wednesday-Too many Middlemen in the Horse Purchases for Government-A man who "helped"- Evidence not sensational, but " influence " was apparently a Requisite.
Then follows the report, which states that:
Twelve others were rejected. Some of these had been sold for war purposes later.
Witness declared that an inspector named Hall had first rejected and later purchased some of the horses.
Four or five of the rejected horses-possibly the whole 12-had been sold through Fallis.
Asked if he had paid any commission to anyone, he said he had given $110 in cash to E. J. Jones, a previous witness. This was after the rejected horses were purchased.
Here is another heading from the Toronto Star:
Jack-Spavined horse sound " in a sense "-Sold as Four Tears Old, Although Age couldn't be estimated-Another was lazy-Would Balk when Heavily loaded-Royal Commission Investigates Purchases.
The Mail and Empire states practically the same thing:
Albert Kee, of Brampton, said that he had purchased 22. horses, but had only been able to dispose of eight of them at the outset to the Government. Subsequently five or six of the animals which had been at first rejected were accepted and sent to the Union Stock Yards in Toronto. He admitted that he had given E. J. Jones $110 after the inspection was over. Pressed for his reason for making the payment, he said that he thought Jones "had
" How had Ire earned it?" he was asked, and he replied, "He helped get the Inspectors to our stables."
The Toronto Star again has a large headline:
Peel County War Horses not up to Standard- Bocal Veterinary says many could not stand up to the Work-Were bought by J. R. Fallis, M.P.P.-Conflicting evidence given as to Price asked by a Bolton Vendor.
I have a long editorial from the Toronto Globe. It is headed: "A Disgrace in Public Life." Many hon. members of this House have no doubt read this article. I have also a few clippings from the Conservative press which it would be in order to read to the members of the House. But I find that the Globe, on December 11, 1915, says:
J. R. Fallis, M.P.P., for Peel, confers with Premier.
What is to bs done about Mr. J. R. Fallis, M.P.P., for Peel, who made handsome profits
buying horses and selling them to the Government for military purposes? The question -is taking up some of the time of Premier Hearst. Mr. Fallis had a lengthy conference with the Premier yesterday. Mr. Richard Blain, M.P., for Peel, was the third party in the conference, and was there presumably to assist Mr. Fallis in presenting his case.
Mr. Fallis greeted the newspapermen amiably, but said, holding up his hand, "I have nothing for you," and left with Mr. Blain. "I have nothing at all to say regarding the conference," said the Premier. No other member of the Cabinet was present with the Premier.
The Toronto Telegram of December 6, 1915, also has a strong editorial demanding the resignation of Mr. Fallis from the Provincial Legislature. The Toronto News strongly condemns the action of this gentleman. I could go on reading clippings to the same effect from leading newspapers throughout the country, but it is hardly necessary. I should just like to call attention to the following from the Toronto World of July 28, 1915:
Shipment of Horses on way to the War.
Two Grand Trunk railway trains loaded with army horses passed through Toronto yesterday en route from Chicago to Montreal. One of these trains had 50 cars, and the other 19, so that in all there were about 1,400 horses. At West Toronto the cars were unloaded the chargers to be exercised and watered, and horsemen who saw them were surprised at the quality of the selection. The horses were bought by the British, military authorities in Chicago, and were rounded up in all the Western States.
A Grand Trunk railway official stated that since the declaration of war more than .80,000 horses have been shipped through Toronto on their way to the front.
Since that date many thousands more horses must have passed through this country from American points. The farmers of this country have a right to expect the Minister of Agriculture and the Prime Minister to help them dispose of the large surplus of horses we have in this country, particularly lin Ontario. But what do we find? Instead of helping the farmer, the Government imposes an embargo which prohibits the farmers of Ontario from shipping their horses just over the line to the State of Michigan, where, after paying $10 duty, they could dispose of these horses to the army buyers in the States. The Government did nothing to help the farmer until practically the very day before Parliament met, when an order in council was passed removing the embargo. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, the farmers of this country are discouraged, and it is incumbent on the Minister of Agriculture or some other member of the Government to an-

nounee to this Bouse and the country whether they intend to give any assistance to this great industry, or 'are going to follow the same unfortunate policy they have pursued in the past. Unless the horse industry is stimulated and encouraged, and the Government finds some way of disposing of the surplus horses we have on hand, the farmers will not raise so many faoTses in 1916 as they did in 1915. I think I have shown that the Government is neglecting this great industry.
You will Temember, Mr. Speaker, that we were told some time ago the Cockshutt Plow Company were not going to raise their prices on agricultural implements because they were too patriotic. In conversation with a farmer the other day who had endeavoured to purchase a Cockshutt machine, I learned that he had been told by one of the Cockshutt agents that their prices had gone up all along the line. This hon. gentleman, who was so patriotic a year ago that he was complimented by the Prime Minister on his stand, has fallen from grace and is raising the price of agri cultural implements to the farmers of this country. It is now rumored that there will be another increase in the tax on agricultural implements. I hope this will not take place. I appeal to the Government to . be satisfied with the taxes they are already levying upon the farmers of this country, and in this connection let me quote from a speech made by the Minister of Labour in the city of Chatham during the Reciprocity campaign of 1911. I am quoting from the Chatham Daily Planet of July 31, 1911. The minister said:
If the farmers went down (to Ottawa) they would get the same answer as the fruit growers got. The duty will remain on hinders though. In other words, the duty will remain on everything the farmer buys, because Sir Wilfred says the duty will remain on manufactured goods. The duty-in other words, the taxes-will be removed in all things you produce and left on all things you have to buy. Is that fair taxation? Why, this agreement is directly in favour of the manufacturer instead of the farmer!
If the question of raising the duty comes up again, I hope the Minister of Labour will practice the same thing that he preached before the Conservative convention at Chatham bn that day.
We have been told by different gentlemen in this House that questions of a contentious nature should not be brought up in the House at the present time. I contend that the matters I have had the privilege of bringing before the House are not con-
tentious in any sense of the word. I have brought these matters to the attention of the ministers of the different departments, because if they give them their serious attention, it will be of great benefit to the farmers of my county and of Canada as a whole, and will greatly assist the manufacturers of my city, and labour generally. We shall then be in a better position to hear our share in the great war that is now going on. I appeal to the Government to give these matters their earnest consideration, and I feel satisfied that if they do so it will greatly assist us in doing what we are all interested in, <* that is to carry this war through to a successful conclusion.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. B. McCURDY (Shelburne and Queens):

THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman states that I made statements which were absolutely and patently untrue. Will he please repeat what I stated and what he says is untrue?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
I think that the point
of order is well taken, and I would like the hon. member to withdraw the expression " untrue."

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
The hon. member for
North Cape Breton has asked me to state in what regard his statements are absolutely and patently incorrect and untrue, and with your permission, Sir, I shall have pleasure in doing so. On page 316 of the Unrevised Hansard, we have the following statement by the hon. member for North Cape Breton:
If the Prime Minister, or anybody else who cares to look the matter up, will turn to the flies of the Halifax Herald-the organ of the right hon. gentleman-of a few days ago, they will find on the front page the picture of a distinguished gentlemen who some time ago fled the country on the pretext that he was going to the war. He will find that this gentleman is back in Nova Scotia with the title of major, and that he is going to he given a battalion in the province of Nova Scotia and sent back to the front. Why was he sent away? Why did he leave the country? He left the country, Sir, because the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia was entering upon a trial at that time, in. which trial he has been found guilty of forgery; in which, in not less than eight cases, he has been found guilty of being an accessory before and after the fact to perjury. He was blacklisted and disqualified by the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, and under that cloud he left the country.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext: That is all true.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
But .he came back-he came back promoted to the position of major, and he is to-day honoured and petted and advanced in the county of Halifax, where the patronage belongs to the Prime Minister, and with the knowledge that the records of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia prove to the hilt everything that I say in respect of him.
Was it fair, was it honourable, was it truthful, for the hon. gentleman to assert that Major Muirhead fled the country on the pretext that he was going to the war? The hon. gentleman cannot deny that when Major Muirhead enlisted for service at the front, there was no charge against him of any kind, and that it was only after he

had been gone for months that his name incidentally figured in an election trial begun many weeks after he had gone overseas. What does the hon. gentleman mean when he says:
Major Muirhead fled the country on the pretext that he was going to the war.
Does he wish to intimate that Major Muirhead has not actually participated in the war? Will he deny that the major has for the last eight months faced death in every form in the defence of the rights and privileges which my hon. friend to-day enjoys in ease and without privation? When the hon. gentleman sgiys:
Major Muirhead left the country, because the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia was entering upon a trial at that time, in which trial he has been found guilty of forgery; and in which, in not less than eight cases, he has been found guiltv of being an accessory before and after the fact to perjury.
The hon. gentleman says something which he has every facility for ascertaining is absolutely and patently untrue.
Mr. MoKENZIE: As a member of this House I have a right to protect myself. I was quoting a matter of record of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, and I consider that the record is open to my hon. friend, and the record will show that 1 was not wrong at all.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
I have not the honour of being as familiar with the practices of that court as is my hon. friend. I have not had the privilege of being a practicing barrister before the courts of Nova Scotia, nor of being a judge of the County Court of Nova Scotia, but I do affirm and my hon. friend cannot controvert my statement that the record of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia- gives no warrant for my hon. friend's assertion that Major Muirhead was ever disqualified by that Supreme Court. Furthermore, at that trial Major Muirhead was not found guilty of perjury; he wlae not even charged with perjury; he had no notice before be enlisted, nor before he went oversea^ that he would figure in any way in the trial, and consequently he had not the slightest opportunity of rebutting references to him which were disclosed as the trial proceeded.
I have the personal assurance of the major himself that had he been present he could have absolutely absolved himself from any blame in connection with the election in question in any way whatever,

and I .accept his statement without the slightest reserve.
The hon. member for North Cape Breton has also deemed it his duty to attack an officer of the 85th Battalion now quartered at Halifax, Dr. Joseph Hayes. He states that Dr. Hayes was made a colonel by the present Minister of Militia. Once again the hon. gentleman's statements are at absolute variance with the facts. He has not even taken the trouble to look up the militia list which is available to every member of this House and to every citizen of this country. Like some other members on the opposite side of the House, he satisfies himself with making assertions although the proof that these assertions are unfounded is open to any person who will take the trouble to seek it. Dr. Hayes received his commission as colonel while the Liberal Minister of Militia was in office six or seven years before 19X1. Does the hon. member for North Cape Breton question the truth of that statement ? Furthermore, Colonel Hayes received his appointment with the 85th Regiment, with which he is now connected, on the recommendation of the officer now commanding that regiment. The name of that officer was mentioned in the House the other day by the Minister of Militia. It is no secret that this officer stated that in the [DOT]election of 1911 he went from Ottawa to Halifax and personally mairsihialled the mem bers of the force there to vote against the present Prime Minister of this country. Colonel Borden has himself stated that he, and he alone, was responsible for the appointment of that officer. Furthermore, Colonel Borden has assured me within the past two weeks that he would not know where to look for a more efficient officer than Colonel Hayes. He says that no -more satisfactory and capable officer could possibly be found.
The hon. member for North Cape Breton criticises Dr. Hayes' appointment as medical officer of the 85th Regiment on the ground that he is a Tory. Why did he not criticise the appointment of Dr. J. A. Sponagle as medical officer of the 25th Battalion on the ground that he is a Grit?
Mr. Speaker, I am gratified to be able to state that no Conservative member in this Parliament, and I believe no Conservative in the country, has ever been guilty of attacking Colonel Sponagle or any
9	p.m. of the numerous other Liberal officers who have received just recognition and promotion on the ground of

their party affiliations. It remained for statesmen of the stature of my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) the hon member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), and the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) to introduce a discordant and unprovoked element into a branch of the service, which, of all others, should be immune from such attacks.
The hon. member for North Cape Breton states that in the county of Halifax, to quote his own words, " the vilest sort of partisans are put at the head of battalions in the highest positions that they can be given." Who are these " vile partisans " of whom he complains? The last battalion to complete mobilization in the province of Nova Scotia is the 85th. Colonel Allison H. Borden, to whom I have already referred, is the first in command'of that regiment. Who is the second in command? Colonel N. H. Parsons, one of the strongest and most active Liberal workers in the county of Kings, a gentleman who quite recently has been addressing Liberal clubs in the Annapolis valley. As to Paymaster Morrison, who, I think, comes from the hon. gentleman's own part of the country, is he to be branded a "vile partisan"? The third officer in command of this battalion is Major Day, whose residence in the United States has removed him from close connection with party associations in this country. He is a splendid type of the expatriated Canadian who in this great emergency have returned to Canada to offer their lives and their all to defend the land of their birth and to ensure the triumph of the cause of civilization.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder what the sturdy soldiers who compose that regiment, particularly those from the county which the hon. member represents, would say to the hon. gentleman, who would state, on his responsibility as a member of this House, that the officers in command of this regiment-Colonel Bordep., Colonel Parsons, Major Day, Paymaster Morrison and the other officers of this popular and efficient staff-are " the vilest sort of partisans." 1 take the responsibility, in their absence and on their behalf, of publicly branding that statement as one absolutely untruthful, unfortunate, and regrettable, one that should not have been made either in this House or out of this House.

speechtext:
I never made the
statement at all.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
I will refer to the hon. gentleman's statement as reported at page 316 of the unrevised Hansard:
But I do charge, in the presence of the Prime Minister, who is a Nova Scotian of whom we are proud, that in the county of Halifax, where I hold him responsible for the patronage, the vilest sort of partisans are put at the head of battalions in the highest possible positions that they can be given.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
That' is absolutely
true.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext: The highest position in the battalion is that of colonel. The latest battalion mobilized in Nova Scotia is the 85th, of which Colonel Borden is the respected, efficient, and honoured commanding officer.

speechtext:
I had no reference to
Colonel Borden.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext: If the hon. member for North Cape Breton does not refer to Colonel Borden, I would ask him to whom he does refer. There are only two regiments quartered in Halifax-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext: If the hon- gentleman wants to know, I had two men in mind, two men blacklisted and condemned by the Supreme Court,-Muirhead and Hayes. These are the only two I had in mind, and I have the record of the Supreme Court to back me up.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
I would suggest to my hon. friend from North Cape Breton, in view of his confession at this time, that he can properly be more particular in the statements he makes in this House. It is not too much to expect that hon. gentlemen who make statements in this House reflecting upon the character of others should be most particular as to what they say. But apparently my hon. friend has imbibed the spirit which has been characteristic of some hon. gentlemen opposite during the course of this debate-that of being ready to make charges and assertions without having the proofs to back them up. The language which my hon. friend used was most explicit. He said that those who hold the highest commissions in these regiments are the vilest sort of partisans. That narrows the case down to the highest officers of the regiment, and, necessarily, so far as I can see, includes the colonels of the 85th and 64th regiments.
I think it is extremely unfortunate and most regrettable that any reference should be made to the politics of the men who are fighting for their country at



the present time. I believe, furthermore, that the references that have been made in this connection are most repugnant to them and most repugnant to the people of the country at large. If there is to be no truce in this Parliament, if there is to be no truce upon the hustings, hon. gentlemen opposite should at least afford to declare a truce with regard to the army itself. Surely men may be allowed to go to the discharge of their duties without being attacked for political affiliations one way or the other.
I can fully appreciate the fact that the provincial by-election, which so emphatically pronounced against Grit methods in the province of Nova Scotia, should he a point of extreme soreness on the part of my hon. friend. More than once has this House listened to the _ lamentations of this modern Jeremiah, who quotes so glibly from Holy Writ. There is a reason for the hon. gentleman's woe. Victoria county is a part of his own constituency, and in the election referred to a Liberal majority of 500 was converted into a substantial Conservative majority. It would appear, therefore, that this election points with unmistakable finger to the goal of political oblivion to which my hon. friend is fast hastening.

speechtext:
My hon. friend would
be glad to meet me or some one else there; my opinion is that he will have sufficient opposition without me.
In his speech ,the hon. gentleman pretended to see indications that the country was returning to the Liberal faith. But I noticed that he had to go a long way from home for consolation. Why does he go so far afield? Why does he not pay attention to his own county of Victoria? Why should he look to the politics of British Columbia, of Manitoba, of even Prince Edward Island, or New Brunswick, for consolation? Why does he not cast his practised eye on the political situation in the province of Nova Scotia? Since the last general election in that province four local contests have been held in counties which have been looked on as having strong Liberal proclivities; to quote the classic language of my hon. friend, they are known as " Grit hives." In every one of these cases-Liberals had represented three of the four of them pre-[DOT] 
vious to the by-elections-the electors pronounced strongly and unmistakably against the party to which my hon. friend belongs.
The political mentor of my hon. friend in the province of Nova Scotia, the Hon. George H. Murray, years ago had a slogan: " Trust the people." The result of the elections to which I have referred has evidently convinced him that he is not altogether safe when he trusts the people. In fact, they say in Nova Scotia that he has changed his motto from " Trust the people " to " Safety first." Would it surprise you, Mr. Speaker, to know that the riding of Victoria has been vacant over a year; that my hon. friend's own constituents were denied the privilege of representation in the last session of the Provincial Legislature, and will be denied that privilege in the coming session, because, forsooth, acting possibly on the advice of the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria, the Premier of that province feels that it is unsafe to trust the people to fill the long existing vacancy in the local House for the county of Cape Breton-
With a splendid show of public spirit the hon>. gentleman pretended to take great pride in the fact that "from the start to the finish of the present war the yeomanry of Canada were ready to sacrifice their lives and property and everything near and dear to them for the general advancement of our country, and to lay everything within their reach upon the altar of our country." I would respectfully commend to my hon. friend the advisability of his profiting iby this splendid example set by the yeomanry of Canada. But while this attitude is being assumed by our yeomanry, what is to be said of those who from their position should he regarded as leaders in this country? It is to be said that, while the yeomanry of Canada are making such splendid and heroic sacrifices for the liberties that we enjoy, the only -people to refuse to make sacrifices are those to whom the people ought to be able to look for leadership in Canada? While the yeomanry of Canada, as my hon. friend says, are sacrificing their all for their country, and brave soldiers like Major Muirhead are holding l-ife itself cheap that the interests of the country may ibe advanced, a small critic gives us the spectacle of being unwilling to forego the opportunity of venting his personal spite and spleen for one moment in the interests, of unity and national strength.

Mr. ARTHUR B. COPP (Westmorland): Mr. Speaker, since the opening of this, the third war session of this Parliament a great many admirable addresses have been delivered by gentlemen on both sides of the House, addresses which, I am sure, as showing the strong feeling of loyalty and patriotism with which members of this House are imbued, must appeal to the country as a whole. I am sure, Sir, that no one could listen to or read those adL dresses without feeling that every member of this House, on which [DOT] ever side of the Speaker he may sit, is prepared, as he has been prepared since the beginning of the war, to do his part to bring this world conflict, which is shaking the British Empire to her very foundations, to a successful and triumphant conclusion.
Mv hon. friends opposite have, at least to a certain degree, questioned the right of 'hon. gentlemen on this side of the House to offer criticism, or to make charges in regard to the administration of the affairs of this country, offering as a reason for taking this course that, because the country is at war, we should not offer criticism and thus embarrass the Government. Now, I am sure that the hon. member Who has just left the chamber, and who addressed the House a few moments ago (Mr. F. B. McCurdy) will pardon me if I do not attempt to answer anything personal he has said in regard to my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie). That is ^ matter in which I do not care to join, even if I had the facts to discuss it intelligently, which I have not, as it is a matter apparently of veracity between the members who represent Nova Scotia on the other side of the House and the hon. members who represent that province on this side.
But I would like to refer to one remark which my hon. friend made. He said it was an unfortunate thing that reference should be made to the politics of men who were engaged in .this war. I agree with the sentiment expressed by my hon. friend, but I would remind him, and other hon. gentlemen opposite, that it can be no greater crime to refer to the politics of men who are engaged in this war than it is for hon. gentlemen opposite to select men because of their politics to fill places in the army service during the war.
My hon. friend spent some minutes in discussing the recent elections in the province of Nova Scotia. Is it possible that my hon. friend has a nightmare in regard to
elections in Nova Scotia or elsewhere at the present moment? Nothing has been said in the debate on the address about elections in the province of Nova Scotia, or in the Dominion of Canada, so far as I have heard, and when the hon. member takes up the time of this House to tell us what has happened in the province of Nova Scotia I should just like to point out that my hon. friend's friends in that province and elsewhere ihave proved very poor prophets indeed in the past.
I wish to refer for a moment or two to the question of our right to criticise the actions of the Government in regard to what we consider questions of great public importance. I lay down the proposition that fair criticism is in order and proper at all times. My hon. friends opposite say that we are offering unfair criticism, and thus embarrassing the Government. My hon. friend from West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) this afternoon, and other hon. gentlemen opposite during the progress of this debate have said, Cannot you find something of which you can say some words of commendation in regard to the Government? Why do you always find fault? Surely some little thing may be said to encourage the Government in regard to public matters on which they are occupied at the present time. Well, Sir, I would not for one moment detract from any member of the Government; but surely the hon. gentlemen who occupy the treasury benches at the present time should be satisfied with the congratulations showered upon them by their hon. friends who sit behind them, and not expect so much congratulation from hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. I am bound to say, Sir, that in many respects the Government have conducted the affairs of this war in an energetic way, and they are entitled to all the credit which their actions may bring to them. But I desire to say to my hon. friends opposite, who claim that we on this side of the House are showering upon them unfair criticism, that it is' just as incumbent upon them to put up a fair defence to their actions as that we should criticise fairly, which we hope to do.
When the other day my hon. friend from the city of St. John (Mr. Pugsley) in the few quiet, well considered remarks which he made to this House, offered the suggestion that some things had not been right, and that the business of this country under the control of the present Administration had not been properly conducted, a terrible wave of disturbance affected our hon.

It was through that gentleman's resigning his position in the Bed Chamber here to accept a more lucrative position that my hon. friend was given easy entrance into this House. Would it not have been better if my hon. friend had frankly told the House the names of all the persons interested in that Becord Foundry and Machine Company? That company was promised a contract of 20,000 shells at the price of the first contract, but when they had prepared their plant they w'eTe given a contract for only 10,000 shells. Was that because Mr. Bobinson or some other gentleman in the company was a Liberal? It is well that we should know the whole facts of the case.
I now come to the Charles Fawcett Manufacturing Company in my own town. While these gentlemen are political opponents of mine, and always have been, there is no concern in the whole province of New Brunswick or even further afield that is better equipped to carry out 'a contract than this firm. The Minister of Militia .has told us that he had great difficulty in getting manufacturers to embark in this business of manufacturing shells-that the Government had almost to go to the banks to get them to finance the manufacturers. That may have been true of some shell-makers, "but on behalf of this organization, let me, say that they [DOT] did not need anybody to finance them, as they were well able to do it themselves. They have been turning out shells now for some considerable time. I am glad that the Fawcett Manufacturing Company' got that order. My objection is that no one has a right to get a contract for making shells at a higher price than is reasonable.
I have a short statement which shows that in the province of New Brunswick the following firms had contracts for shells: Cornwall and York Cotton Mills, St. John, N.B., 25,000 shTapnel shells, at $3.80 each; Charles Fawcett Company, 20,000	4.5

$6.70, and 20,000 at $6; the Smith Foundry Company, Fredericton, N.B.,	20,000	4.5
howitzer shells ' at $6. The Cornwall and York Cotton Mills got $3.80 'apiece for machining 'and assembling these shells. About the same time another, firm, the Electric Steel and Metals ' Company, of Welland, which I understand is largely controlled by Mr. Carnegie, a member of the Shell Committee, got an order for 25,000 shells at $5 apiece; that is an advance of $1.20 over the other firm. The Canadian Car and Foundry Company of Montreal, of which I believe Senator Curry is president and one of the largest owners of stock, also got an order at the same time for making shells at $5.15 apiece. I should like to know why all these firms were not paid the same price for manufacturing shells. At Sackvilile the Charles Fawcett Company got a contract for 20,000 4.5 howitzer shells at $6 apiece. The Canadian Car and Foundry Company got an order for 50,000 shells at $6.70. Why the increased price? I claim that that is absolute evidence that there was some influence somewhere that caused the Shell Committee to give these contracts out at these different prices. We go a little further and we find that the James Flemming concern of St. John, N.B., got a contract for shells at $6 the same prices as the Fawcett Company received. The Montreal Locomotive Company of Montreal, Que., got orders for 10,000 shells at $6.70 and 150,000 at $6 per shell. The Maritime Foundry and Machine Company of Chatham got a contract for
20.000	shells at $6. The Macdonald Thresher Company of Stratford got a contract for
16.000	shells at $6. We find Messrs. EMc-Avity and Sons of St. John, N.B-, supplying 10,000 of the same size of shell to which I have referred at $6.70 and 20,000 at $6, and the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company of New Glasgow, owned by a member of the Shell Committee, got their first contract for 25,000 shells at $6.70, and a second for 25,000 at $6.50 at practically the same time that these other concerns were being paid $6. I draw the attention of the House to these facts, and with these facts before us we naturally expect explanations why different prices have been paid to different manufacturers of shells getting contracts at the same time.
