I grant there are many considerations, and there were many considerations in regard to the letting of these contracts by the Shell Committee. The Fawcett Company is at Sackville, which is a small place, and it is not so closely in touch with the Shell Committee as the Canadian Car and Foundry .Company, of which Senator Curry is president. If we get down to brass tacks, that is the condition, and that is why these' gentlemen are getting more for their contracts than are the people in Sackville, St. John, Chatham and Fredericton.
My hon. friend the Minister of Militia attempted yesterday, in a very cordial, genial, and pleasant way, to explain the condition of affairs in regard to matters that are being looked after by himself, or by his adopted child, as he calls the Shell Committee. I do not intend to follow all the arguments made by my hon. friend the Minister of Militia. He glossed over, very creditably indeed to himself, many things, and he kept the House in good humour, to say the least, while he was giving as little ' information as he possibly could in regard to this Shell Committee. For one thing, Sir, you will note that he spent a considerable amount of time in telling this Parliament and the people of this country that, irrespective of the fact that this is a Conservative Administration, or, to be more correct, a Conservative-Nationalist Administration, it apparently selected seventy-five or eighty per cent, of Liberals to do its work throughout this country. Did my hon. friend seriously expect-I do not wonder that the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) laughs-this House to believe that that has been the case during the past three years? Not at all. It has been just the reverse. I am not here to criticise hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to that point, nor to say anything in regard to the political affiliations of the men whom they appoint to do their work if they will only do it well; but there has been a great deal of discussion and many extracts have been placed upon Hansard during this debate in regard to this matter. My hon. friends opposite took refuge behind an editorial in the Ottawa Free Press, in which an attack was made on the hon. member for the city of St. John because of his attitude towards the Shell Committee, and submarines, and other things in which this Government and this country is interested. I have no quarrel with the Free Press in regard to its

Fitzsimmons that he would see to it that he got a contract?
I have said that one of the four requirements for the proper carrying on of Canada's part in this war is that of proper officers to conduct and control the men on the field of battle. From the information which I have, I understand that when the Canadian soldiers go over to England they are placed under the command of British officers. Against this I have not a word to say; but I do wish to say a word to the Minister of Militia dn regard to the officering of the men while they are under training. I -make this complaint not for the purpose of making political capital or of indulging in political criticisms. I -have said at different times during the course of my remarks that I care not whether a man is a Grit or Tory so long as he is doing his best in connection with this great conflict. But I do say that many young boys, sons of the more wealthy people, are being sent to military schools and are getting commissions, while some of the older men who have been in training for years, are occupying positions as privates. In the course of their duties they are meeting with these young boys, who must appear to them somewhat as my hon. friend the Minister of" Militia described the barristers the other day, with their hair parted in the middle, and with pencil and paper, seeking contracts.
I do not claim this because they are Liberals, but I do say that if these old soldiers, veterans and warriors, who have had the advantage of education, training and experience, were given a better show when officers are being selected, it would be very much more to the credit of the department and would result in much greater benefit to the training camps.
I am not so big a farmer as my hon. friend the .member for Carleton (Mr. Car-veil) ; I am not, I suppose, as good a lawyer, but I have had some experience with the hay question. I sell some hay myself, and I think I know whereof I speak so far as hay is concerned. I listened with a great deal of astonishment to the remarks of the hon. member for Carleton upon this subject. The hon. Minister of Agriculture, if any man in Canada is supposed to do it, is supposed to protect the farmers, who are really producing the wealth of Canada at this time; and we would expect that he would accord them fair treatment. Well, I knew that this contract had been given, and I 
knew the effect it had in my county. When the hon. member for Carleton made the direct charges in this House in regard to hay, a storm took place in the mind of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture. I have only a passing acquaintance with the hon. minister; I do not purpose entering into the personal quarrel between him and the hon. member for Carleton. I hold no brief for the hon. member for Carleton; I am not here to say whether his parliamentary conduct was proper or improper, or whether my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture did himself justice in the language which he used in reference to the hon. member for Carleton. My position, however, is different from that of the hon. member for Carleton. The Minister of Agriculture seems to think that the trouble between the hon. member for Carleton and the Atlantic Hay Company was occasioned by a personal quarrel. I have a personal and intimate acquaintance with the gentleman *who has charge of the Atlantic Hay Company, B. F. Smith. I am not here to say an unkind word or to make an unkind reference to that gentleman in so far as the hay contracts are concerned. I am bound to say that I do not blame him very much for getting as much as he could, within reasonable scope, for the hay he had to sell. I do charge that the Minister of Agriculture did enter into an improvident bargain and an improvident contract in regard to the supply of hay from the province of New Brunswick to the Imperial Government. I think I can show why. In the first place, when the Department of Agriculture, as agent or trustee for the Imperial Government, wanted to obtain from the province of New Brunswick a supply of
15,000	tons of hay, amounting in value to about $350,000, in round figures, it would seem to me that the cautious and businesslike way to deal with the matter would be to ask for tenders from the different hay dealers, so that the farmers would have an opportunity of tendering for the supply of this hay at the lowest possible price.
My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture attempted to defend his department against the charges made iby my hon. friend from Carleton; but you may search Hansard from the beginning of his remarks to the close and you will not find any indication that he asked any other firm in the province of New Brunswick concerning the price of hay. What was his answer? He said they wanted a certain quantity of hay, and he decided to make -a deal with one

man. Let ns take the hon. minister at his word that it was more reasonable and proper for the department to deal with one man in that matter. If the hon. minister thinks it is necessary to deal with one man and pay him an exorbitant price for hay he is placing- himself before this House and before the country in a most unfavourable. light. This hay was to be shipped from West St. John, one of the winter ports of Canada. There is no mistaking the facts; there is no getting around them; there is no use in saying -that this thing is wrong and that is wrong; the farmer has the hay to -sell. I may tell the hon. minister that last year I -sold hay. I have hay to sell this year. Last year I sold my hay for $15 per ton; the merchant who bought it resold it, and made his profit which was not less than $1. He sent the hay to the United States, I understand.
What happened this year? The hon. minister says that -he made this contract with the Atlantitc -Hay Company at the price of $23 f.o.b. West St. John. The distance from Woodstock to St. John is about the same as from Sackville, my shipping port, to St. John, and from Sackville the freight, to -St. John costs from $1.65 to $1.75 per ton. The price we p-ay for pressing is $1.25, sometimes $1.30; but on an -average the pressing and freight to St. John run about $3 per ton. It costs $3 to compress the hay; that is wh-at the hon. Minister of Agriculture admitted in his remarks yesterday. That makes $6 as the cost from the time the hay leaves the farmer's barn till it lands f.o.b. -cars at West St. John. Now, to-day they are buying that hay in my town or in the vicinity of Sackville, and shipping it at Sackville for $12 and in some oases as low as $11 per ton. But let us say $12; it was up to $13, and dropped back again to $12. Add the $6 which it takes to get -the hay to West St. John, and you have $18. Now, the contractors	of the hon. minister are
getting $23 per ton, which means that they are making a profit of $5 on every ton of hay that goes from Sackville to West St. John. They are making a profit of $5 per ton on 15,000 tons, or a net profit of $75,000. There is no getting around these figures. There are no excuses; there is no answer to the charge made. When my hon. friend from Carleton charged the Minister of Agriculture as the head of his department, and the man responsible for the conduct of that department, with taking $45,000 or $50,000 out of the pockets of the
farmers of New Brunswick, or out of the coffers of the Imperial Government, he left him to choose whichever horn of the dilemma he car-ed to take. My hon. friend from Carleton put the amount very fairly, because as a matter of fact they are buying a very large portion-I will not say more than half-but a good portion of the hay for at least $13 per ton and in many cases less.
The hon. Minister of Agriculture, from his place yesterday, stated that he always wanted to do what was fair and right for the agricultural people of this country. We all remember the cry of patriotism and production that' passed over this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific last year-It was all very well to talk about patriotism and production. The farmers responded to the demand for production, and what is the result? The Minister of Agriculture has entered into an improvident contract with a firm of political supporters in the province of New Brunswick which is taking from $2 to $3 and in -many cases more on every ton of hay from the farmers of that province. The hon. minister said he was ready to defend his action from first to last. He charged the hon. member for Carleton with striking below the belt. Let me tell the Minister of Agriculture that if my hon. friend from Carleton struck below the belt in defence of the farmers of New Brunswick, my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture struck below the belt when he entered into that contract, and sacrificed the interests of the farmers of New Brunswick to the tune of $50,000 to which they were entitled. That is the condition of affairs as regards the hay question in that province, and, although the Minister of Agriculture attempted to defend himself, he utterly failed to answer the charges made by my hon. friend from Carleton. His own confession is the very best evidence that he did wrong. He told us that he had cancelled the contract at the demand or request of my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B., because he had concluded it was an improvident contract. That i-s the confession he made. He found it was not a proper contract. We have heard read the letters that passed between the Minister of Agriculture and the firm which got the contract. I can discuss this question without any personal feelings against the firm. The minister charged the hon. member for Carleton with entertaining some such feeling against the firm, but I have a very -warm feeling for the farmers in my own county, and proper-

ly so. When the minister entered into that contract and immediately afterwards, the Goyernment put an embargo upon the exportation of hay to the United States, what did it mean? It meant that they were taking from $2 to $3 per ton from th< farmers in that section of the country. ] it was necessary for the Imperial Government to have all the hay in the province of New Brunswick, or in that particular section of the province, in order to carry on the war, the farmers were prepared to allow them to take the hay, and they were willing to make the price $13 or $12 or $10. But they were not and are not prepared to make sacrifices in order to put $3 or $4 per ton into the pockets of certain individuals. I know that I am voicing the sentiments of every one of tlhe farmers of my county when I say that they are prepared to put in their hay to this Government if the Government will take it themselves and do away with the middlemen provided they are prepared to accept the hay at the price mentioned by my toon, friend. But they are not prepared to sacrifice their interests for the benefit of others.
I hope that the Minister will not, in the future, for his own benefit, for his own credit, attempt to make the people of the country believe that he has made a proper contract and one that is in the interest of the farmer. The best proof that he has made an improvident contract is that he has changed it because, for, to use an expression often heard, the coon came down. He has changed his contract, and in that connection my hon. friend from Carleton says he does not know his man. I am not going to go that far, but my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture, in making that announcement, at the same time makes the admission that he has made a contract at too high a price. Now, he has told the Atlantic Hay Company that in the handling of this hay they will only be allowed to make a dollar a ton.' He has opened a situation that I doubt very much if the hon. gentleman, with all the ability that he may have, will be able to carry through.
I am anxious to see what kind of a bill of expenses will be made up for buying this hay and these presses and other incidentals; it will be interesting to have it brought before Parliament and see what final adjustment is made. It reminds me of the story of the man who got a bill from his attorney. The attorney put a great many items in this long bill-so much for 
drawing the bill of costs, so- much for drawing the defence, and so much for drawing something else. This was so astonishing to the client that when he got his bill that he wrote at the bottom of it: You forgot to put in anything for drawing your breath. When the Minister of Agriculture gets his bill from the Atlantic Hay Company he will find many items that he did not expect. Surely the Minister of Agriculture has been in this House and has been allied with his friends long enough not to be so innocent as to expect the House and the country to believe that with a contract entered into with the Atlantic Hay Company, that contract being signed, sealed and delivered, he is going to be able to compel these people to come forth with. their books of account and cheque stubs and make a settlement, and at the same time give a fair deal to the farmers of the 'country. It is absolutely impossible.
There was an altercation between the Minister of Agriculture and my hon. friend from Carleton with regard to the conditions of a contract for the supply of hay in which my hon. friend from Carleton was interested some years ago. I know nothing about that. I was not a member of the House at that time, nor was my hon. friend from Carleton. But there was one mistake that the minister did make, and that was where he claimed the spread between the purchase price of the hay from the farmer and the amount paid by the Government was $9.50 under the present contract, whereas the spread between the price paid the farmer by the company with which my hon. friend was associated and that paid by the Government was $9. There was a mistake of $1 per ton, and $1 makes a grea* deal of difference when you come to consider the question of the profit on a ton of hay. But, in so far as this present company is concerned, $1 is neither here nor there when it is making a profit of $4 or $5 a ton. It seems to me that my hon. friend the minister did not get very far in the defence of his actions in regard to the hay question. May I ask the Minister of Agriculture if he will not reconsider this matter. I care not about Mr. Smith's contract; it does not affect us very much, although he has been driven from his own county and has come down to our county. But, I ask the minister to consider well and carefully whether it is necessary, with the amount of hay required about secured, to continue the embargo on hay to the United States.

Then he should lift the embargo, and give us entrance to the United States markets at a fair competitive price, or else he should say to this man: You must show that so much has been paid for this hay, so much for freight and so much for expenses, and we will give you so much per ton. I would request you hot to leave this contract in the hands of this man in the slipshod way in which it now is. Reduce the price, because there are no ifs and ands about it. If the man is getting $2 or $3 per ton too much under his contract, cut it down to a fair price and give the people of the province of New Brunswick a fair show in regard to their hay.
There is just one other matter that I will refer to, and it is one which is dealt with in the gracious speech that His Royal Highness delivered at the opening of this House.
I refer to the question as to the extension of the life of this Parliament. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) made some reference to that paragraph in the Speech from the Throne. My hon. friend discussed the question in a serious manner. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries rather replied in a strain of levity, saying that my hon. friend from St. John had given an interview out West to the effect that it would be a deplorable thing to have an election, but, now that the scene had changed, it was a serious thing to extend the life of Parliament. I think it is a most serious thing. That does not mean that I am opposed to an extension of the life of this Parliament by any means. I think it is a serious thing at any time to' change the Constitution of this country under which the people have lived and of which they are very jealous indeed. The question is:	Is the situation of so serious a nature
that it is a proper thing to do? When the measure comes before this House I think the Government will find that every mem, ber on this side at least is prepared to give it that consideration that it deserves. But, to say that it is a serious matter is not going too far. It is a matter between ourselves and our constituents. The Constitution gives those who happened to be elected at the beginning of a parliamentary term the privilege of retaining their seats for five years if the Government choose to continue the life of Parliament for that time. This is a delicate matter for every member of this House to consider as between himself and his constituents; he must ask himself
the question whether or not he should vote himself another year in Parliament. If the wishes of a member, in his personal capacity as the representative of his county, only had to be consulted, I do not think there would be any question in his mind, because I do not know of any man who is anxious to run an election when he has a seat in Parliament if he can retain that seat another year. Therefore, I repeat that it is a serious matter that every member in this House must decide for himself, and when the resolution comes before the House I am sure that it will be given the very best consideration of hon. gentlemen, at any rate upon this side of the House.
I realize that I am a young member of . this House so far as experience goes, and I must apologize for having detained the House so long, but when one is gathering facts for a speech one's notes are increasing all the time, and sometimes become too voluminous. I have felt it my duty to bring these matters to the attention of Parliament. I believe the people of this country desire more information in regard to these matters. My hon. friend has been accused of making insinuations based on newspaper 'clippings. In regard to that I would say that a man who reads the . newspapers must be more or less influenced by what he reads. A man reads the newspapers to get the view of the public on these matters, and in regard to the charges which have been made against the Shell Committee I am bound to say that practically all the large and influential newspapers in the country, both Liberal and Conservative, have for some months been criticising the Shell Committee, if they have not actually made charges against it. One can hardly attend church without hearing the subject treated from the pulpit. Surely that is evidence enough that the public is keenly interested in this matter. I sincerely trust that whatever may be the outcome of the charges that have been made, every member of this House will see to it that his best thought and best endeavour is given to the proper carrying on of the war to a successful conclusion; and that, we trust, will not be very long delayed.
On motion of Mr. Sinclair, the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Hon. Robert Rogers, the House adjourned at 10.37 p.m.

Monday, January 31, 1916.
